q: Every thermometer uses a physical property that varies with ____.
e: Thermometers operate by measuring a physical property that changes predictably and continuously with temperature.

q: This property is referred to as the ____ property of the thermometer.
e: A thermometric property is any physical property that varies linearly and continuously with temperature, enabling temperature measurement.

q: For example, the thermometric property of a liquid-in-glass thermometer is the ____ of the liquid.
e: Liquid-in-glass thermometers rely on the predictable thermal expansion of the liquid inside the capillary tube as temperature changes.

q: The liquid-in-glass thermometer consists of a thin glass bulb joined to a ____ tube with a narrow bore which is sealed at its other end.
e: The capillary tube's narrow bore ensures that small changes in liquid volume result in visible changes in the liquid thread length.

q: When the bulb becomes warmer, the liquid in it expands more than the bulb so some of the liquid in the bulb is forced into the ____.
e: Differential expansion between the liquid and the glass forces the liquid up into the narrow capillary tube, indicating a temperature rise.

q: The thinner the bulb wall is, the ____ the response of the thermometer will be when the temperature changes.
e: A thinner bulb wall reduces thermal resistance, allowing heat to transfer more quickly and resulting in a faster thermometer response.

q: The liquid used usually contains ____ (or) coloured alcohol.
e: Mercury and coloured alcohol are the two most common liquids used in liquid-in-glass thermometers due to their distinct thermometric properties.

q: Alcohol has a lower ____ than mercury so it is more suitable for low-temperature measurements.
e: Alcohol remains liquid at much lower temperatures than mercury, making it ideal for measuring cold environments.

q: Thermocouple thermometers are electrical thermometers which make use of the ____ that develops when two different metals are in contact.
e: Thermocouples operate on the Seebeck effect, where a temperature difference between two dissimilar metal junctions generates a measurable voltage.

q: One of the junctions is maintained at ____ and the other junction is used as the temperature probe.
e: A reference junction is typically kept at a known constant temperature, such as 0℃, to calibrate the voltage reading of the probe junction.

q: Because of the small size of a thermocouple junction, thermocouple thermometers are used to measure ____ changing temperatures.
e: The low thermal mass of the small junction allows thermocouples to respond almost instantaneously to rapid temperature fluctuations.

q: In addition, they can be used to measure much ____ temperatures than liquid-in-glass thermometers.
e: Thermocouples can withstand and accurately measure extremely high temperatures that would melt or vaporize liquid-in-glass thermometers.

q: Resistance thermometer uses the fact that the electrical resistance of a metal (e.g platinum) wire ____ with temperature.
e: In a resistance thermometer, the electrical resistance of the metal wire increases predictably as the temperature rises.

q: A resistance thermometer can measure temperatures accurately in the range ____ to 1200℃ and best for steady temperatures, but it is bulky.
e: Resistance thermometers offer high accuracy over a wide range from -200℃ to 1200℃, though their bulkiness limits certain applications.

q: Thermometric substances can be ____, liquids (or) gases.
e: Thermometric properties can be observed and utilized in all three states of matter: solids, liquids, and gases.

q: They have physical properties that vary continuously and ____ with temperature.
e: For a substance to be a good thermometric material, its chosen physical property must vary both continuously and linearly with temperature.
